claim: Bisphosphonate drugs target the skeleton and are used globally for the treatment of common bone disorders.
source: Bisphosphonates drugs target the skeleton and are used globally for the treatment of common bone disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement about bisphosphonates that draws from established scientific consensus about their clinical use.

claim: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates act by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in bone-resorbing osteoclasts.
source: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates act by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in bone-resorbing osteoclasts but, surprisingly, also appear to reduce the risk of death from pneumonia.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of action of N-BPs.

claim: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates appear to reduce the risk of death from pneumonia.
source: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates act by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in bone-resorbing osteoclasts but, surprisingly, also appear to reduce the risk of death from pneumonia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: A fluorescently labelled bisphosphonate is internalised by alveolar macrophages in vivo.
source: We overturn the long-held belief that these drugs act only in the skeleton and show that a fluorescently labelled bisphosphonate is internalised by alveolar macrophages and large peritoneal macrophages in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A fluorescently labelled bisphosphonate is internalised by large peritoneal macrophages in vivo.
source: We overturn the long-held belief that these drugs act only in the skeleton and show that a fluorescently labelled bisphosphonate is internalised by alveolar macrophages and large peritoneal macrophages in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A single dose of zoledronic acid in mice is sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Furthermore, a single dose of a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) in mice was sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages, causing the build-up of a mevalonate metabolite and preventing protein prenylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A single dose of zoledronic acid causes the build-up of a mevalonate metabolite in tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Furthermore, a single dose of a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) in mice was sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages, causing the build-up of a mevalonate metabolite and preventing protein prenylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data showing IPP/DMAPP accumulation in Figure 2b.

claim: A single dose of zoledronic acid prevents protein prenylation in tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Furthermore, a single dose of a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) in mice was sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages, causing the build-up of a mevalonate metabolite and preventing protein prenylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the unprenylated Rab protein assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: One dose of bisphosphonate enhanced the immune response to bacterial endotoxin in the lung.
source: Importantly, one dose of bisphosphonate enhanced the immune response to bacterial endotoxin in the lung and increased the level of cytokines and chemokines in bronchoalveolar fluid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: One dose of bisphosphonate increased the level of cytokines and chemokines in bronchoalveolar fluid.
source: Importantly, one dose of bisphosphonate enhanced the immune response to bacterial endotoxin in the lung and increased the level of cytokines and chemokines in bronchoalveolar fluid.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex analysis data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Bisphosphonates may boost immune responses to infection in the lung.
source: These studies suggest that bisphosphonates, as well as preventing bone loss, may boost immune responses to infection in the lung and provide a mechanistic basis to fully examine the potential of bisphosphonates to help combat respiratory infections that cause pneumonia.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates are used as the frontline treatment for post-menopausal osteoporosis.
source: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) are a class of bone-seeking drugs used worldwide as the frontline treatment for disorders of excessive bone resorption such as post-menopausal osteoporosis and cancer-associated bone disease (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 2011.

claim: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates are used as the frontline treatment for cancer-associated bone disease.
source: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) are a class of bone-seeking drugs used worldwide as the frontline treatment for disorders of excessive bone resorption such as post-menopausal osteoporosis and cancer-associated bone disease (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 2011.

claim: N-BPs bind rapidly to the skeleton by virtue of their avidity for calcium ions.
source: By virtue of their avidity for calcium ions, N-BPs bind rapidly to the skeleton, where they are internalised by bone-degrading osteoclasts (Russell et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russell et al., 2008 and Rogers et al., 2020.

claim: N-BPs are internalised by bone-degrading osteoclasts.
source: By virtue of their avidity for calcium ions, N-BPs bind rapidly to the skeleton, where they are internalised by bone-degrading osteoclasts (Russell et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russell et al., 2008 and Rogers et al., 2020.

claim: N-BPs disable osteoclast function by inhibiting the enzyme farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway.
source: Intracellularly, N-BPs disable osteoclast function by inhibiting the enzyme farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway (van Beek et al., 1999; Dunford et al., 2001), thereby preventing the post-translational prenylation of small GTPase proteins necessary for osteoclast function (Luckman et al., 1998; Fisher et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Beek et al., 1999 and Dunford et al., 2001.

claim: Inhibition of FPP synthase by N-BPs prevents the post-translational prenylation of small GTPase proteins necessary for osteoclast function.
source: Intracellularly, N-BPs disable osteoclast function by inhibiting the enzyme farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway (van Beek et al., 1999; Dunford et al., 2001), thereby preventing the post-translational prenylation of small GTPase proteins necessary for osteoclast function (Luckman et al., 1998; Fisher et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luckman et al., 1998 and Fisher et al., 1999.

claim: N-BP therapy has benefits beyond preventing bone loss.
source: There is increasing evidence that N-BP drugs, such as zoledronic acid (ZOL), have benefits beyond preventing bone loss (Center et al., 2020), and, unexpectedly, N-BP therapy has recently been linked to reduced risk of mortality from pneumonia (Colón-Emeric et al., 2010; Sing et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Center et al., 2020.

claim: N-BP therapy has been linked to reduced risk of mortality from pneumonia.
source: There is increasing evidence that N-BP drugs, such as zoledronic acid (ZOL), have benefits beyond preventing bone loss (Center et al., 2020), and, unexpectedly, N-BP therapy has recently been linked to reduced risk of mortality from pneumonia (Colón-Emeric et al., 2010; Sing et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Colón-Emeric et al., 2010 and Sing et al., 2020.

claim: ZOL therapy reduced the risk of death by 28% compared to placebo infusion in a randomised, controlled trial of >2000 hip fracture patients.
source: In a randomised, controlled trial of >2000 hip fracture patients, ZOL therapy reduced the risk of death by 28% compared to placebo infusion (Lyles et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lyles et al., 2007.

claim: ZOL-treated patients were less likely to die from pneumonia than placebo-treated subjects in retrospective analysis.
source: Retrospective analysis also suggested that ZOL-treated patients were less likely to die from pneumonia than placebo-treated subjects (Colón-Emeric et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Colón-Emeric et al., 2010.

claim: A population-based, observational study showed a significant reduction in risk of pneumonia and pneumonia mortality in hip fracture patients that had received N-BP therapy compared to no treatment or other osteoporosis medications.
source: Recently, a 'real-world' population-based, observational study of hip fracture patients aged 50 years or above also showed a significant reduction in risk of pneumonia and pneumonia mortality in hip fracture patients that had received N-BP therapy compared to no treatment or other osteoporosis medications (Sing et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sing et al., 2020.

claim: Similar findings regarding N-BP benefits were reported in the post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial of ZOL in women over the age of 65 years.
source: Similar findings were reported in the post hoc analysis of a randomised controlled trial of ZOL in women over the age of 65 years (Reid et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reid et al., 2021.

claim: Pneumonia is the most frequent cause of admission to ICU.
source: Pneumonia is the most frequent cause of admission to ICU, and a study of long-term patients in respiratory ICU revealed a significant reduction in mortality in people treated with the N-BP pamidronate compared to those without treatment (Schulman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge.

claim: A study of long-term patients in respiratory ICU revealed a significant reduction in mortality in people treated with the N-BP pamidronate compared to those without treatment.
source: Pneumonia is the most frequent cause of admission to ICU, and a study of long-term patients in respiratory ICU revealed a significant reduction in mortality in people treated with the N-BP pamidronate compared to those without treatment (Schulman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schulman et al., 2016.

claim: A retrospective cohort study of ICU subjects showed a 59% reduction in mortality in patients treated with bisphosphonate prior to hospitalisation.
source: Furthermore, in a retrospective cohort study of ICU subjects, we showed a 59% reduction in mortality in patients treated with bisphosphonate prior to hospitalisation (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of N-BPs on pneumonia and in ICU patients are unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms underlying the surprising beneficial effects of these drugs on pneumonia and in ICU patients are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Respiratory diseases constitute the most common cause of death globally.
source: Globally, respiratory diseases constitute the most common cause of death, and thus, therapies that boost the immune response to common lung infections are urgently needed.
evidence: This is a statement of established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus are the main cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
source: Bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus are the main cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge.

claim: Bacterial pathogens underlie severe complications of viral respiratory disease that can significantly increase morbidity and mortality.
source: Importantly, these pathogens also underlie severe complications of viral respiratory disease that can significantly increase morbidity and mortality.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge.

claim: Influenza-related mortality is often associated with pneumonia caused by co- or secondary bacterial infection.
source: For example, influenza-related mortality is often associated with pneumonia caused by co- or secondary bacterial infection (Morris et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morris et al., 2017.

claim: Cultured macrophages have the ability to internalise N-BP by endocytosis.
source: We previously reported that cultured macrophages and tumour-associated macrophages in vivo, like osteoclasts, have the ability to internalise N-BP by endocytosis (Thompson et al., 2006; Junankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2006 and Junankar et al., 2015.

claim: Tumour-associated macrophages in vivo have the ability to internalise N-BP by endocytosis.
source: We previously reported that cultured macrophages and tumour-associated macrophages in vivo, like osteoclasts, have the ability to internalise N-BP by endocytosis (Thompson et al., 2006; Junankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2006 and Junankar et al., 2015.

claim: AMΦ play an important role in lung homeostasis and the initial immune response to respiratory infection.
source: Given the important role of AMΦ in lung homeostasis and the initial immune response to respiratory infection (Byrne et al., 2015; Crane et al., 2018), we focused on whether these cells are capable of internalising a systemically administered, fluorescently labelled analogue of ZOL (AF647-ZOL).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2015 and Crane et al., 2018.

claim: AF647-ZOL did not inhibit protein prenylation compared to the parent N-BP (ZOL) when tested in cultures of bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Like most other fluorescently labelled N-BPs (Roelofs et al., 2010), AF647-ZOL did not inhibit protein prenylation compared to the parent N-BP (ZOL) when tested in cultures of bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM; Figure 1a), but can be used to track drug uptake by cells in vivo (Junankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and a citation to Roelofs et al., 2010.

claim: AF647-ZOL can be used to track drug uptake by cells in vivo.
source: Like most other fluorescently labelled N-BPs (Roelofs et al., 2010), AF647-ZOL did not inhibit protein prenylation compared to the parent N-BP (ZOL) when tested in cultures of bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM; Figure 1a), but can be used to track drug uptake by cells in vivo (Junankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Junankar et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 90% of cells in BAL were AMΦ in the absence of immune challenge in mice.
source: In the absence of immune challenge in mice, approximately 90% of cells in BAL were AMΦ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: >98% of AMΦ in BAL samples were clearly labelled with AF647-ZOL 4 hr after i.v. administration.
source: Importantly, >98% of AMΦ (TCRβ-B220-CD11blo/-CD11chiF4/80+) in BAL samples were clearly labelled with AF647-ZOL 4 hr after i.v. administration (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1b-d.

claim: 80% of cells obtained by peritoneal lavage consisted of PMΦ under baseline conditions.
source: Under baseline conditions, 80% of cells obtained by peritoneal lavage (PL) consisted of PMΦ (B220- TCRb- Siglec-F- Ly6G- CD11b+ F4/80+), most of which were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ, with a less abundant population of CD11b+F4/80int small PMΦ (Ghosn et al., 2010; Cassado Ados et al., 2015; Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to Ghosn et al., 2010 and Cassado Ados et al., 2015.

claim: Most peritoneal macrophages were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ, with a less abundant population of CD11b+F4/80int small PMΦ.
source: Under baseline conditions, 80% of cells obtained by peritoneal lavage (PL) consisted of PMΦ (B220- TCRb- Siglec-F- Ly6G- CD11b+ F4/80+), most of which were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ, with a less abundant population of CD11b+F4/80int small PMΦ (Ghosn et al., 2010; Cassado Ados et al., 2015; Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to Ghosn et al., 2010 and Cassado Ados et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 80% of peritoneal cells incorporated AF647-ZOL after a single i.v. dose.
source: Similar to BAL cells, approximately 80% of peritoneal cells incorporated AF647-ZOL after a single i.v. dose (Figure 1f), the majority of which (99%) were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: 99% of AF647-ZOL-positive peritoneal cells were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ.
source: Similar to BAL cells, approximately 80% of peritoneal cells incorporated AF647-ZOL after a single i.v. dose (Figure 1f), the majority of which (99%) were CD11bhiF4/80hi large PMΦ (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1g and h.

claim: CD11b+F4/80int small PMΦ incorporated negligible amounts of fluorescently labelled ZOL.
source: In contrast, the CD11b+F4/80int small PMΦ incorporated negligible amounts of fluorescently labelled ZOL (Figure 1i).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: N-BP can be efficiently internalised in vivo by tissue-resident macrophages outside the skeleton, including AMΦ in the lung and LPMΦ in the peritoneal cavity.
source: In addition to the well-described uptake of N-BP by osteoclasts in bone (Rogers et al., 2020; Coxon et al., 2008), these findings clearly demonstrate that N-BP can also be efficiently internalised in vivo by tissue-resident macrophages outside the skeleton, including AMΦ in the lung and LPMΦ in the peritoneal cavity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and citations to Rogers et al., 2020 and Coxon et al., 2008.

claim: Small amounts of ZOL can accumulate in soft tissues in rodents.
source: Despite the rapid bone-targeting property of N-BPs, it has been shown in rodents that small amounts of ZOL can accumulate in soft tissues (Green and Rogers, 2002); however, the concentrations that can be achieved are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Green and Rogers, 2002.

claim: The cytoplasmic build-up of IPP and its isomer DMAPP is a reliable feature of intracellular N-BP action in cells.
source: To determine whether tissue-resident macrophages can incorporate sufficient N-BP in vivo to have a pharmacologic effect, we analysed two biochemical outcomes that, together, are reliable features of intracellular N-BP action in cells (Rogers et al., 2020): (i) the cytoplasmic build-up of the upstream metabolite isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and its isomer dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) (Räikkönen et al., 2009); and (ii) reduced production of the isoprenoid lipid geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP), with the consequent accumulation of unprenylated small GTPase proteins including those of the Rab and Rho superfamilies (Luckman et al., 1998; Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rogers et al., 2020 and Räikkönen et al., 2009.

claim: Reduced production of GGPP with the consequent accumulation of unprenylated small GTPase proteins is a reliable feature of intracellular N-BP action in cells.
source: To determine whether tissue-resident macrophages can incorporate sufficient N-BP in vivo to have a pharmacologic effect, we analysed two biochemical outcomes that, together, are reliable features of intracellular N-BP action in cells (Rogers et al., 2020): (i) the cytoplasmic build-up of the upstream metabolite isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and its isomer dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) (Räikkönen et al., 2009); and (ii) reduced production of the isoprenoid lipid geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP), with the consequent accumulation of unprenylated small GTPase proteins including those of the Rab and Rho superfamilies (Luckman et al., 1998; Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rogers et al., 2020 and Luckman et al., 1998, and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: IPP/DMAPP was undetectable in extracts of BAL or PL cells from saline-treated mice.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis showed that IPP/DMAPP was undetectable in extracts of BAL or PL cells from saline-treated mice, but there was a clear increase in the level of IPP/DMAPP in BAL and PL cells collected 48 hr after a single i.v. injection of ZOL (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was a clear increase in the level of IPP/DMAPP in BAL and PL cells collected 48 hr after a single i.v. injection of ZOL.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis showed that IPP/DMAPP was undetectable in extracts of BAL or PL cells from saline-treated mice, but there was a clear increase in the level of IPP/DMAPP in BAL and PL cells collected 48 hr after a single i.v. injection of ZOL (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: ZOL treatment resulted in a marked accumulation of unprenylated Rab proteins in BAL and PL cell samples.
source: Importantly, ZOL treatment also resulted in a marked accumulation of unprenylated Rab proteins in BAL and PL cell samples (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro prenylation assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The development of a much more sensitive in vitro prenylation assay now allows the detection of subtle effects on protein prenylation in cells outside the skeleton that may internalise much smaller quantities of N-BP.
source: However, the development of a much more sensitive in vitro prenylation assay (Ali et al., 2015) now allows the detection of subtle effects on protein prenylation in cells outside the skeleton that may internalise much smaller quantities of N-BP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ali et al., 2015.

claim: Systemic administration of N-BP has pharmacological activity outside the skeleton in healthy mice.
source: Together with the evidence for uptake of N-BP by AMΦ and large PMΦ and (Figure 1), these findings demonstrate unequivocally that systemic administration of N-BP has pharmacological activity outside the skeleton in healthy mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: A single dose of ZOL is sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages (AMΦ and PMΦ), causing a build-up of IPP/DMAPP metabolites and an accumulation of unprenylated small GTPase proteins.
source: We show that a single dose of ZOL is sufficient to inhibit the mevalonate pathway in tissue-resident macrophages (AMΦ and PMΦ), causing a build-up of IPP/DMAPP metabolites and an accumulation of unprenylated small GTPase proteins – characteristic hallmarks of N-BP action (Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2 and a citation to Rogers et al., 2020.

claim: The findings overturn the long-standing textbook paradigm that N-BP drugs act only in the skeleton.
source: Although still to be confirmed in humans, our findings overturn the long-standing textbook paradigm that N-BP drugs, which have been in clinical use for several decades (Russell, 2011), act only in the skeleton.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The transient acute phase response was previously thought to be caused by the accumulation of IPP in circulating monocytes, which then activates Vγ9Vδ2-T cells to produce TNFα and IFNγ.
source: This was previously thought to be caused by the accumulation of IPP in circulating monocytes, which then activates Vγ9Vδ2-T cells to produce TNFα and IFNγ (Roelofs et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roelofs et al., 2009.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages, such as AMΦ and large PMΦ, are a more likely source of the IPP responsible for the activation of Vγ9Vδ2-T cells.
source: Our findings suggest that tissue-resident macrophages, such as AMΦ and large PMΦ, are in fact a more likely source of the IPP responsible for the activation of Vγ9Vδ2-T cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing IPP accumulation in tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Loss of protein prenylation in cultured monocytes promotes the formation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in increased caspase-1-mediated processing of pro-IL-1β following LPS stimulation.
source: We recently reported that loss of protein prenylation in cultured monocytes promotes the formation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in increased caspase-1-mediated processing of pro-IL-1β following bacterial endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide [LPS]) stimulation (Skinner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Skinner et al., 2019.

claim: ZOL treatment alone did not alter the percentage, total number or viability of AMΦ recovered in BAL samples.
source: ZOL treatment alone did not alter the percentage, total number or viability of AMΦ recovered in BAL samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), nor had any effect on the levels of cytokines/chemokines in BAL fluid (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZOL treatment alone had no effect on the levels of cytokines/chemokines in BAL fluid.
source: ZOL treatment alone did not alter the percentage, total number or viability of AMΦ recovered in BAL samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), nor had any effect on the levels of cytokines/chemokines in BAL fluid (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: I.n. LPS administration in ZOL-treated mice resulted in a significant increase (2.5- to 5.0-fold) in the production of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα, G-CSF, GM-CSF and chemokines CXCL1, CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in BAL fluid compared to control mice.
source: However, i.n. LPS administration in ZOL-treated mice resulted in a significant increase (2.5- to 5.0-fold) in the production of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα, G-CSF, GM-CSF and chemokines CXCL1, CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in BAL fluid compared to control mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex analysis data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The increase in cytokine and chemokine release was not associated with changes in the percentage or total number of AMΦ, or in the number or viability of cells in BAL fluid.
source: This increase in cytokine and chemokine release was not associated with changes in the percentage or total number of AMΦ, or in the number or viability of cells in BAL fluid (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: I.p. LPS challenge of ZOL-treated mice resulted in a significant elevation in IL-1β in peritoneal fluid, and CCL2 and CCL5 in serum, compared to controls.
source: I.p. LPS challenge of ZOL-treated mice also resulted in a significant elevation in IL-1β in peritoneal fluid, and CCL2 and CCL5 in serum, compared to controls (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex analysis data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Peritoneal cells from ZOL-treated mice produced almost three times more IL-1β upon ex vivo stimulation with LPS and nigericin than cells from control mice.
source: Furthermore, peritoneal cells from ZOL-treated mice produced almost three times more IL-1β upon ex vivo stimulation with LPS and nigericin (a well-described NLRP3 activator) (Figure 3d) than cells from control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: IL-1β is primarily produced by monocytes/macrophages.
source: IL-1β is primarily produced by monocytes/macrophages (Kany et al., 2019), the predominant cell type in PL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kany et al., 2019.

claim: Macrophages are the most likely source of IL-1β in PL fluid.
source: Thus, our results strongly suggest that macrophages are the most likely source of IL-1β in PL fluid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the knowledge that macrophages are the predominant cell type in PL.

claim: Treating mice with ZOL did not cause IL-1β release from peritoneal cells stimulated ex vivo with LPS in the absence of nigericin.
source: Importantly, treating the mice with ZOL did not cause IL-1β release from peritoneal cells stimulated ex vivo with LPS in the absence of nigericin (Figure 3d), and this is in accord with our previous finding that inhibition of the mevalonate pathway alone does not trigger NLRP3 inflammasome assembly but enhances its activation (Skinner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3d and a citation to Skinner et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of the mevalonate pathway alone does not trigger NLRP3 inflammasome assembly but enhances its activation.
source: Importantly, treating the mice with ZOL did not cause IL-1β release from peritoneal cells stimulated ex vivo with LPS in the absence of nigericin (Figure 3d), and this is in accord with our previous finding that inhibition of the mevalonate pathway alone does not trigger NLRP3 inflammasome assembly but enhances its activation (Skinner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Skinner et al., 2019.

claim: AMΦ are one of the first lines of defence against common respiratory tract infections.
source: AMΦ are one of the first lines of defence against common respiratory tract infections (Byrne et al., 2015), and inhibition of the mevalonate pathway in these cells may help boost the initial response to bacterial as well as viral lung infections by a variety of routes (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Byrne et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of the mevalonate pathway in AMΦ may help boost the initial response to bacterial as well as viral lung infections.
source: AMΦ are one of the first lines of defence against common respiratory tract infections (Byrne et al., 2015), and inhibition of the mevalonate pathway in these cells may help boost the initial response to bacterial as well as viral lung infections by a variety of routes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Uptake of N-BP into cells causes the accumulation of IPP/DMAPP, which activates human Vγ9Vδ2-T cells.
source: First, uptake of N-BP into cells causes the accumulation of IPP/DMAPP (Figure 2b), which activates human Vγ9Vδ2-T cells (Thompson and Rogers, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and a citation to Thompson and Rogers, 2004.

claim: Vγ9Vδ2-T cells are non-conventional T cells with potent antibacterial and antiviral activity that recognise phosphoantigens, including IPP, derived from the mevalonate or DOXP pathways in bacterial pathogens.
source: Vγ9Vδ2-T cells are non-conventional T cells with potent antibacterial and antiviral activity that recognise phosphoantigens, including IPP, derived from the mevalonate or DOXP pathways in bacterial pathogens (Tanaka et al., 1995; Jomaa et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 1995 and Jomaa et al., 1999.

claim: There is considerable interest in the use of N-BP-expanded γ,δ-T cells as an immunotherapy for cancer.
source: There is considerable interest in the use of N-BP-expanded γ,δ-T cells as an immunotherapy for cancer (Clézardin and Massaia, 2010; Tanaka, 2020) as well as viral diseases (Juno and Kent, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clézardin and Massaia, 2010 and Tanaka, 2020.

claim: There is considerable interest in the use of N-BP-expanded γ,δ-T cells as an immunotherapy for viral diseases.
source: There is considerable interest in the use of N-BP-expanded γ,δ-T cells as an immunotherapy for cancer (Clézardin and Massaia, 2010; Tanaka, 2020) as well as viral diseases (Juno and Kent, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Juno and Kent, 2020.

claim: N-BP-expanded Vγ9Vδ2-T cells reduce disease severity and mortality from influenza A virus (IAV) infection in humanised mice.
source: Indeed, N-BP-expanded Vγ9Vδ2-T cells reduce disease severity and mortality from influenza A virus (IAV) infection in humanised mice (Tu et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tu et al., 2011 and Zheng et al., 2015.
